lesson.title: Where attention goes

lead.text: Start with something you have probably done. You are reading in a café when someone at the next table begins an interesting story, and a minute later you realise you have read the same line three times. Your senses were taking in the page the whole time. Your attention was somewhere else.

At every moment your senses take in far more than the mind can use. Attention is how it chooses. It follows one stream, such as the story at the next table or the line you are reading, and turns the others down. This is selective attention, and it is what lets you follow one voice in a noisy room.

The choice has a price. What you are not attending to is dealt with far less thoroughly than what you are attending to. How far that can go is shown by an experiment that has been repeated many times.

In the experiment, viewers watched a short film of two teams passing basketballs, one team in white shirts and one in black. They were asked to count the passes made by the white team. Partway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the middle of the players, thumped their chest and walked out again. The gorilla was on screen for several seconds.

When viewers were asked afterwards whether they had noticed anything unusual, around half had not seen the gorilla at all. They were not careless or short-sighted. Many had counted the passes accurately. Their attention was on the white shirts and the ball, and an object in plain view, which they did not expect and were not looking for, never registered.

This is inattentional blindness: failing to notice a clearly visible, unexpected object because attention is directed at something else. Looking at a thing and seeing it are different, and attention is what links the two.
Here is a class demonstration with the same film. The counts show how many of the people counting passes missed the gorilla.

Now return to the eight cards. Call the sums task A, in which you judge whether a digit is odd or even, and the word puzzles task B, in which you judge whether a letter is a vowel or a consonant. Every trial takes some time. When you move from A to B, or from B to A, the mind has to drop one set of rules and pick up the other, and that takes extra time called the switch cost. Repeating the same task has no such cost.

To count the switches in a sequence, look at each pair of neighbouring trials and count the pairs where the task changes. The first trial is not a switch, because nothing came before it. AAB has one switch, between the second A and the B. ABAB has three.

The total time for a sequence is the number of trials times the time per trial, plus the number of switches times the switch cost. The figure shows two orders of eight trials with the same trial time and the same switch cost.

afterFigure.text: The alternating order has a switch between every pair of neighbouring trials. The blocked order has just one, in the middle. Both orders contain the same work, and the difference in time comes entirely from the switches.

lead.text: Read a sequence from left to right and compare each trial with the one before it.

steps.headline: Find the time for AABAB when each trial takes 400 ms and each switch adds 100 ms.

workedSteps.text: Count the changes of task: A to B, B to A, A to B.
Add the trial time and the switch time.

lead.text: Now use the digit and letter judgements from the cards. Each trial takes 600 ms, and each change of task adds 200 ms.

The two orders of the eight cards have the same number of trials, so the time spent on the cards themselves is the same. Only the number of switches differs. Doing the sums first and the words after, in the order AAAABBBB, has a single switch. Alternating has one between every pair of neighbouring trials, and each of those switches adds the same cost.

People can reduce a switch cost by getting ready. If you know which task comes next, you switch faster. Preparation shrinks the cost without removing it, which is why answering messages while writing a report takes longer than it feels. Each message is a switch away from the report, and the return to the report is another.
Each trial takes 600 ms and each change of task adds 200 ms. Both orders contain eight trials.

The same cost appears outside the laboratory. Driving is a task, and so is working through a problem in your head. A driver who does both is not doing them at the same instant. Attention moves between them, and each move is a switch.

Watson and Strayer asked whether anyone escapes this. They put 200 people in a driving simulator and gave them a demanding memory-and-arithmetic task to do while they drove. They then checked whether either task got worse compared with doing it alone.

For nearly everyone it did. A very small group, whom the researchers called supertaskers, showed no measurable cost on either task. Because supertaskers are so rare, a person who feels sure they multitask well is much more likely to be one of the others.
Some drivers in the study showed no cost at all from doing a second demanding task. The counts are in the picture.

lesson.orientation: Measure what selective attention misses and what switching between tasks costs.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You have eight cards to work through. Four are sums and four are word puzzles, and every card takes about the same time as any other. You can do all the sums and then all the words, or you can alternate, a sum and then a word, to keep things varied.

It seems that the order should make no difference, since the cards and the work are the same. The mind is not a set of drawers that open and close for nothing, though. It points at one job at a time, and what it is pointed at shapes both what you notice and how quickly you work.

This lesson starts with what happens when attention is pointed hard at one thing, including a failure that happens in plain view. Then it returns to the cards and puts a price on every change of job. It ends with a study of people who tried to do two demanding things at once while driving.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say why attending to one thing can hide another, and work out what switching between tasks costs in time.

recap.keyIdea: Attention is selective, so unattended things can be missed even when they are in view, and every change of task adds a switch cost. Multitasking is mostly alternating.

blocks.text: Back at the eight cards, the order is no longer arbitrary. You found that 14 of 30 people, 46.7%, missed the gorilla while counting passes. Alternating ABABABAB took 6,200 ms against 5,000 ms in blocks, a loss of 1,200 ms, and only 2.5% of drivers showed no cost from a second task.

recap.nextHook: Attention decides which signals get in, and the next lesson asks how the mind combines the ones it does receive, starting with a block that looks 50 mm tall and feels 56 mm through thick gloves.

questions.prompt: Each trial takes 500 ms and each change of task adds 150 ms. How long does AABBAABB take, in milliseconds?
hints: Look for each place where A is followed by B or B by A.
There are eight trials at 500 ms each.
Add the switch costs to 4,000 ms.
questions.onCorrect: Trial time plus switch time, with only the changes of task counted as switches.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the trials. Add the cost of each change of task.
Read the sequence again. It changes task fewer times than that.

questions.prompt: An observer concentrating on a task fails to see a clearly visible but unexpected object. What is this failure called?
hints: It is a kind of blindness caused by where attention was directed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inattentional blindness: the object was visible but not attended.

questions.onCorrect: The object was visible but not attended, so it went unseen. That is inattentional blindness.

misconceptions.feedback: Change blindness is missing a change between two views. Here the object was never attended.

questions.prompt: Each trial takes 500 ms and each change of task adds 150 ms. How many milliseconds faster is AAAABBBB than AABBAABB?
hints: Both have eight trials, so only the switches differ.
Count the switches in each sequence.
Multiply the difference in switches by the cost of one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: AABBAABB has 3 switches and AAAABBBB has 1. The 2 extra switches cost 2 × 150 = 300 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Equal trials mean only switches differ: two extra switches at the same cost each.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole switch cost of the mixed order. The blocked order has a switch too.
That is the cost of one switch. How many extra switches are there?

questions.prompt: Which order will take less time?
hints: Each card takes the same time. What else is going on between cards?
Think about what happens in your head each time the kind of job changes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sums first, then words: the job changes only once, so the mind reconfigures only once.

choices.label: Swapping between a sum and a word each time
They will take the same time.

questions.onCorrect: Changing job costs time on top of the work itself. You reasoned out a switch cost before it had a name.

misconceptions.feedback: Every swap makes you change the kind of job. That is extra work beyond the cards themselves.
The cards take equal time, but the changes between jobs do not come free.

questions.prompt: Which statement does inattentional blindness support?
hints: The object in the study was in plain view.

acceptedIdeas: Looking at something does not guarantee that you see it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Looking is not seeing: an object in plain view can be missed if attention is elsewhere.

choices.label: People with poor eyesight cannot see unexpected things.
Looking at something does not guarantee that you see it.

questions.onCorrect: Attention decides what you notice, so something in plain view can still be missed.

misconceptions.feedback: The viewers had ordinary eyesight. The cause was where their attention was.
Many did see it. It was missed only by those attending elsewhere.

questions.prompt: In a class demonstration, 14 of the 30 people counting basketball passes failed to notice the gorilla. What percentage missed it? Give one decimal place.
hints: Divide the number who missed it by the number watching.
The denominator is 30.
Convert 14/30 to a percentage and round to one decimal place.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 14/30 = 0.4667, or 46.7%, close to the 46% Simons and Chabris reported.

questions.onCorrect: Divide those who missed it by all who watched: nearly half failed to notice something in plain view.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of people who missed it. Turn it into a percentage of everyone watching.
That is the share who noticed it. The question asks for the share who missed it.

questions.prompt: How many switches are in the sequence ABBA?
hints: A switch is a change from one task to the other.
Read the sequence from left to right.
Count the places where the letter changes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A to B, then B to A: two switches. B to B is not a switch.

questions.onCorrect: A switch is a change of task: A to B and B to A. Repeating B costs nothing extra.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only one of the two changes. Read the sequence left to right.
That counts the gap between every pair of trials. Repeats are not switches.

questions.prompt: In the sequence AABAB, why are there 3 switches in 5 trials?
hints: Look at each pair of neighbouring trials. Is the task different?

acceptedIdeas: Only a change from one task to the other counts, and the first two trials are the same task.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only a change of task is a switch. Two As in a row are not.

choices.label: Every trial after the first counts as a switch.
Every second trial is a switch.
Only a change from one task to the other counts, and the first two trials are the same task.

questions.onCorrect: Only changes of task count. A repeated task adds no switch cost.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be four, and it ignores that the first two trials match.
Switches depend on the sequence, not on every other trial.

questions.prompt: Each trial takes 600 ms and each change of task adds 200 ms. How long does the sequence ABABABAB take in total, in milliseconds?
hints: Count the places where the letter changes.
Every trial costs 600 ms; each switch adds 200 ms.
Add 8 × 600 to the number of switches × 200.
questions.onCorrect: Trial time plus switch time: eight trials, and a switch before every trial except the first.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the trials. Each change of task adds more.
Eight trials make only seven changes. Count the gaps where the task changes.

questions.prompt: Each trial takes 600 ms and each change of task adds 200 ms. How many milliseconds longer does ABABABAB take than AAAABBBB?
hints: Both sequences have eight trials, so only switches differ.
Count the switches in each sequence.
Multiply the difference in switches by 200 ms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ABABABAB has 7 switches and AAAABBBB has 1; the extra 6 switches cost 6 × 200 = 1,200 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Both have eight trials, so only the switches differ: six more switches, each at the same cost.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cost of one switch. How many more switches does the alternating order have?
That is the whole switch cost of the alternating order. The blocked order has a switch too.

questions.prompt: In the study, 5 of 200 drivers showed no cost from doing a demanding task while driving. What percentage is that?
hints: Divide the supertaskers by the total tested.
The total is 200.
Convert 5/200 to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Five in two hundred is a very small share: nearly everyone paid a cost for doing two things.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count of drivers. Turn it into a percentage of all those tested.
That is the share who showed a cost. The question asks about those who showed none.
